alalal-e90040-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 9: whether the same thing can be simultaneously known and believed.

alalal-e90040-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's chapter 'Post haec quaeri solet', since faith concerns the non-apparent.

alalal-e90040-d1e129.summary: Proposes that the same thing can be known and believed at once.

alalal-e90040-d1e137.summary: First argument: sensory cognition is lower than intellectual, yet neither excludes the other and the higher often aids the lower; so faith and science need not exclude each other.

alalal-e90040-d1e153.summary: Second argument: a lesser light does not remove a greater, so neither faith nor science removes the other.

alalal-e90040-d1e164.summary: Third argument: philosophers who came to faith, like Justin, Dionysius and Apollophanes, knew by natural reasons that God is one; if faith voided science they would have to forget those reasons, which is false.

alalal-e90040-d1e186.summary: Fourth argument: we daily seek natural reasons, not based on faith's principles, by which faith can be defended, and these can generate a habit of science; so the same can be known and believed.

alalal-e90040-d1e204.summary: Fifth argument: Job 12:7 ('ask the beasts') and Psalm 18:2 ('the heavens declare') show that natural reasons about God can be drawn from creatures.

alalal-e90040-d1e220.summary: Sixth argument: the Virgin knew by experience that she conceived by the Holy Spirit without male seed and also believed it.

alalal-e90040-d1e234.summary: Introduces the common objections to the contrary.

alalal-e90040-d1e239.summary: First: the Gloss on John 14:2 says the Lord goes so as not to be seen, hidden so as to be believed; so hiddenness from reason makes belief.

alalal-e90040-d1e264.summary: Second: faith concerns the non-apparent, and what is known is very apparent.

alalal-e90040-d1e275.summary: Third: Hugh says science is above faith, so it voids faith, since the imperfect is useless when the perfect comes (1 Corinthians 13:10).

alalal-e90040-d1e298.summary: Fourth: in matters of opinion, science voids opinion, so also faith.

alalal-e90040-d1e307.summary: Fifth: as love of God for himself, when it comes, voids love of God for temporal things, so faith voids consent based on reason.

alalal-e90040-d1e324.summary: Sixth: the Samaritans told the woman they no longer believed because of her word but because they had heard and knew (John 4:42); the woman stands for knowledge by reason, which is voided when faith comes.

alalal-e90040-d1e346.summary: Solution: faith and science concern the same thing but not in the same respect, so neither voids the other, and the first arguments are granted in this sense; faith does not assent because of reason, but reason is there under faith, and likewise science.
claims: Faith and science can concern the same thing in different respects without excluding each other.
Faith does not assent because of reason; reason operates under faith.

alalal-e90040-d1e364.summary: Reply to the first objection: the Gloss means the Apostles' assent is more meritorious if hidden from bodily sight, which is true, since faith's merit is greater the less proof reason provides.

alalal-e90040-d1e384.summary: Reply to the second: in the respect in which faith concerns an article, there can be no science or reason about it, as often explained.

alalal-e90040-d1e397.summary: Reply to the third: Hugh speaks of the science of truth that is face-to-face vision, not of rational science in this life, which is much less certain than faith.
claims: Rational science in this life is less certain than faith.

alalal-e90040-d1e415.summary: Reply to the fourth: Albert thinks it false, since opinion and science can concern the same thing, especially in different people, and even in the same person, though he relies more on science.

alalal-e90040-d1e429.summary: Reply to the fifth: one who loves God only for temporal things is not without mortal sin; one who loves God for himself and temporal things only for use, not enjoyment, need not have that love voided.

alalal-e90040-d1e447.summary: Further: if one loves God above all but temporal things immoderately below God, the analogy fails, since that love is venial sin absorbed by perfect charity, whereas science is meritorious and no sin at all.

alalal-e90040-d1e467.summary: Reply to the sixth: the allegory proves only the point about faith's assent in relation to reason that has already been conceded.

alalal-e90040.summary: Article 9 asks whether the same thing can be both known and believed. For: lower and higher cognitions coexist, converted philosophers kept their proofs that God is one, natural reasons defend faith, creatures declare God, and the Virgin knew by experience what she believed. Against: faith concerns the hidden and non-apparent, and science, as more perfect, would void it, as it voids opinion. Albert holds that faith and science can concern the same thing, but not in the same respect, so neither voids the other. Faith does not assent because of reason; reason works under faith. Hidden things make faith more meritorious. In the respect in which faith holds an article there is no science of it. Hugh's 'science above faith' means face-to-face vision, while rational science in this life is less certain than faith.
claims: Faith and science can concern the same thing in different respects without excluding each other.
In the respect in which faith holds an article, there is no rational science of it.
Rational science in this life is less certain than faith; only beatific vision surpasses faith.
